newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ex-Soviet states to mark Chernobyl anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Soviet states to mark Chernobyl anniversary.

text.p: Valery Khodymchuk died 11 years ago on Saturday but he has not been buried and he never will be.

The 34-year-old was the first victim of the world's worst nuclear disaster at Ukraine's Chernobyl plant north of Kiev. This week Khodymchuk's friends and colleagues unveiled a gravestone in Moscow's Mitino cemetery to his memory.
"He is the only person whose burial site is the fourth bloc (at Chernobyl)," said Gennady Rusakovsky, a station worker who survived the blast in the early hours of April 26, 1986.
"I saw him five minutes before the explosion. When the explosion happened the building he was in fell through. I never saw him again," he told Reuters.

This weekend tens of thousands of people across the former Soviet Union will mark with tears, prayers and protests the anniversary of the disaster that unleashed a lethal radioactive cloud over Europe and blighted millions of lives.
Eleven years on, a serious lack of cash is hampering the efforts of the Soviet Union's successor states to deal with Chernobyl's legacy.
"The tasks (of tackling the social and medical consequences of the disaster) are very far from resolved," said Russia's Emergencies Ministry in a press statement on Friday.
"The basic problem is irregular and insufficient financing," it said, adding this resulted in cutbacks in aid to the affected population and big delays in the payment of social benefits.
Khodymchuk's widow, who lives in the Ukrainian capital Kiev, told Reuters she struggles to support herself and her family with a monthly pension for her husband of just $100.
Russia is focusing its resources on the four regions near the Ukrainian border most badly affected by the radioactive fallout, Mikhail Faleyev of the Emergencies Ministry said.

In these areas, the incidence of cancers and other diseases is many times greater than elsewhere in Russia, Faleyev told a news conference. The Communist authorities, following an ingrained habit of keeping bad news secret, took days to come clean and alert people to the disaster.

In neighbouring Belarus, the anniversary has become a catalyst to protests against hardline President Alexander Lukashenko. Thousands of anti-Lukashenko demonstrators are expected in the capital Minsk on Saturday, as they did last year.
Lukashenko, who has clamped down on demonstrations and had many opposition leaders detained in recent months, has suggested the protesters go to Chernobyl to mark the anniversary.

On Friday, local authorities announced they had opened a case against extremists planning a coup attempt. Minsk's prosecutor said they had arrested just one man however for passing out pamphlets calling for violence on Saturday.
Downwind from Chernobyl, Belarus was very badly affected by the explosion, which blew the reactor's roof off.

Ukraine, which like Belarus won its independence from Moscow in 1991, has drawn up a plan with the Group of Seven leading industrialised Western countries to stabilise the crumbling sarcophagus built around the fourth reactor after it blew up.

President Leonid Kuchma has promised to close down the remaining reactors completely by the year 2000 in return for $3.1 billion of Western credits. The G7 is expected to decide on funding arrangements for the plan at its June summit.

This week Ukrainian health officials said a many members of the clean-up teams sent in after the disaster were sick, as were their children, partly because of shortages of pure, unradiated food in the contaminated zones surrounding Chernobyl.

Ukrainian estimates show about two million of its 52 million people live in contaminated areas around Chernobyl, including 479 people who have returned voluntarily to live in the 30-km (19-mile) exclusion zone around the nuclear site.
Many stay because they fear their homes will be looted.
"I had everything, now I have nothing," said Viktor Prisyazhnyuk, who briefly abandoned his home in the zone last December and returned to find it completely looted.
Nuclear experts say the entire zone should remain uninhabited for the next three centuries.
